reference.source: Williams Hematology / WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours
clinicalPearls: An uncommon autoimmune haemolytic anaemia caused by a biphasic IgG autoantibody, the Donath-Landsteiner antibody, usually directed against the P antigen
It most often occurs in children after a viral infection and produces acute, sometimes dramatic, intravascular haemolysis
Classic features are cold-triggered episodes of haemoglobinuria with fever, back or abdominal pain and pallor
The Donath-Landsteiner test is diagnostic: the antibody binds red cells and fixes complement in the cold, then triggers lysis on rewarming
The direct antiglobulin test is typically positive for complement (C3d) and negative for IgG because the IgG antibody elutes on warming
Unlike cold agglutinin disease, haemolysis is predominantly intravascular and the antibody is IgG rather than IgM
In children the disorder is usually acute and self-limiting, and management is supportive with warmth and transfusion when needed
reference.pathophysiology: Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria is mediated by a biphasic IgG autoantibody, the Donath-Landsteiner antibody, classically specific for the P blood group antigen. In the cooler peripheral circulation the antibody binds red cells and fixes early complement components; when the cells return to core body temperature the complement cascade proceeds to completion, producing complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis and haemoglobinuria. The antibody itself detaches on warming, which is why the direct antiglobulin test detects complement rather than IgG. The disorder most often arises transiently after viral or other infections in children.
additionalDifferentials: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency with acute haemolysis
Transfusion or other acute intravascular haemolysis
additionalInvestigations: Direct antiglobulin test with monospecific C3d and IgG reagents
Blood film and haemolysis markers including free haemoglobin
Reticulocyte count, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin and bilirubin
Screening for a preceding or concurrent infection
redFlags: Rapid, severe haemoglobin fall with haemodynamic instability
Marked haemoglobinuria with risk of acute kidney injury
Recurrent episodes suggesting a persistent or secondary cause
Haemolysis in an adult prompting evaluation for underlying malignancy or syphilis
reference.prognosis: Post-infectious paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria in children is usually acute and self-limiting with full recovery once the trigger resolves; supportive care and keeping the patient warm are generally sufficient.
pitfalls: Confusing it with cold agglutinin disease and misdirecting therapy
Not requesting the specific Donath-Landsteiner test, so the diagnosis is missed
Allowing the patient or blood products to be cold, precipitating further haemolysis
Overlooking rare chronic adult forms historically linked to syphilis
management: Manage supportively, as the post-infectious childhood form is usually acute and self-limiting with full recovery
Keep the patient warm and avoid cold exposure to prevent the biphasic Donath-Landsteiner antibody from binding red cells
Transfuse for symptomatic anaemia, warming both the patient and the blood via an in-line warmer
Provide intravenous fluids to maintain renal perfusion during intravascular haemolysis and haemoglobinuria
Identify and treat any preceding or concurrent infection that triggered the episode
Monitor haemoglobin, reticulocytes and haemolysis markers until recovery, reserving corticosteroids or other immunosuppression for rare persistent or chronic disease
